chapter: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
title: New Orleans bricklayer-musicians and Standard Oil work in Baton Rouge
summary: Fritz and Roque came from New Orleans to work as bricklayers at Standard Oil, where steady pay made music a sideline.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Why didn't Isadore Fritz(?) ever record or anything? Did he die early, or...?
Oh yeah, those guys... In fact... In the first place, they had no facilities. Fritz never went no place. And there wouldn't be no place in Baton Rouge for him to record.
He went to New Orleans, didn't he, for a while?
Well, he was from New Orleans, I believe.

Because I'm thinking that George was born just around six years before you, and he told me that he used to listen to Isadore Fritz. I can't remember George being in Baton Rouge for any time, so Fritz must have...
No, Fritz came from New Orleans, around there, and so did Manuel Roque. I know Manuel was from New Orleans.
Why did they... I mean, I know you can't answer why they moved. But was there more opportunity for playing clarinet in Baton Rouge than New Orleans?

No, not really. A lot of New Orleans musicians stayed in New Orleans because they made a living, or an existence... Most of them had little extra jobs, though. They made... Johnny Dodds, the clarinet player, Kid Ory said he worked on the railroad part-time. But a lot of

them came to Baton Rouge to work at the Standard Oil Company, which paid pretty good money, because it was a steady job where they worked every day. And they had a... They was bricklayers; actually that was their trade -- Fritz and Manuel Roque.

Both of them. And Standard Oil had a deal where they had these big coke ovens they called them, where they had to be built up... They'd burn out, and they had to have bricklayers all the time to replace them.
So in other words, they got steady employment if they came to Baton Rouge.
And they could fool with their clarinet playing in their off time.
And music was strictly a sideline.
